data.description:
#### The HACKnight showcase is the traditional after-event of DINAcon, and an excellent way to get started as a contributor to open source.

This year we are showcasing the [Hack Apertus](https://hackapertus.ch) events of Bern/Liebefeld 2026, with projects built with the Apertus LLM family on three case challenges. Over 200 projects from the virtual hackathon can be browsed at [hackapertus.ch/projects/search](https://hackapertus.ch/projects/search).

During our traditional "apéro with keyboards", we welcome people and machines of all skill levels, inspired by open [hackdays](https://opendata.ch/events/) and [hackergartens](https://www.hackergarten.net/). On this page we post challenges, issues and activities from projects presented at [DINAcon](https://dinacon.ch/). We also provide a quick introduction to anyone interested in learning more about the activities of [CH Open](https://www.ch-open.ch/). All relevant proposals to start, improve or support open source projects are welcome. The entry is free, and so is the shell 🖪 and beer 🍺 thanks to all the partners and supporters of DINAcon! [Please see the official DINAcon program for more details](https://dinacon.ch/en/program/). A conference ticket is NOT required if you are only joining us for the HACKnight.

data.longtext:
The University of Bern challenges participants to decipher archival records with Apertus. Instead of full-text search over digitised pages, the goal is to turn source records into structured findings and searchable knowledge: select an archive collection, ask a question, and inspect the supporting quotation beside the answer. Solutions preserve source references and original wording, make uncertainty visible, and support human review and reusable exports. Apertus is the foundation of the archival AI workflow, from interpreting transcriptions to proposing structured findings and source-grounded answers.

Case partner: University of Bern. Submissions at the Hack Apertus hackathon (October 2026) included CORA (AI-ready, provenance-tracked metadata for Swiss Federal Archives records), Stapfer Evidence Explorer (question answering over the 1799 school survey), ArchAI (extraction, verification and cited answers) and Oldif (intelligence fusion for historical archives).

data.longtext: CORA turns records of the Swiss Federal Archives into AI-ready, provenance-tracked metadata with Apertus v1.5. For each document Apertus writes a résumé of at most 3 sentences (can be turned off) and decides whether it is a primary, secondary or tertiary source and of which type. It also completes Gallica-style metadata (creator, publisher, commissioner, dates of creation, publication, update and archiving, place in the archive), assesses the preprocessing the record needs (transcription normalization, structure extraction, schema harmonization, entity linking, date/geo parsing, anonymization verification) and traces the document's story on a map.

data.longtext:
Stapfer Evidence Explorer combines a structured dataset of the 1799 school survey, an Apertus-powered question-answering application and a human-review dashboard.

How it works: Python converts the supplied SQL database into searchable data, preserving 2,250 transcriptions and 92,524 answer rows. Apertus helps select relevant survey fields, Python retrieves and links the evidence, and Apertus generates a cited answer. LIVE uses real Apertus8B inference; only the labelled DEMO mode uses scripted responses. Draft reference answers never enter the model as hints. Assisted review found 38/50 correct answers for Apertus versus 47/50 for Qwen32B. These are diagnostic results, not independent held-out accuracy. Document-quality auditing and verified page references remain pending.

data.longtext:
Our code cleans up the transcriptions, matches 857 of 858 signatures to the archive database, finds place names and pulls out numbers. Apertus rewrites the question and writes an answer with sources, and then our code checks it. Every number has to show up in the cited text, all counting and adding is done by code, and if the archives don't have the answer, ArchAI says so. In our tests it ranked the right source first for 92.4% of 380 questions and turned down 23 of 24 questions it couldn't answer.

**Hack Apertus Bern/Liebefeld — Winner (EDUCATION)**

**Team:** Kirtan Padh, Philipp Baumann, Dhruv Mulay, Pratik Waghmode, Jorgo Ananiadis
**Challenge:** Deciphering Swiss archives with Apertus — University of Bern
**The WIN:** CHF 3,500 + qualified to compete for the Main «Hack Apertus» Award in St.Gallen (May 2027) · ElevenLabs 3 months Scale tier ($897 value/team member, 1.8M credits/mo) · $200 Hugging Face credits · DINAconCH conference ticket, T-shirt & demo table

**What the team built:**
ArchAI turns three open Swiss archive datasets into one AI-ready, provenance-preserving dataset and serves it through a cited Q&A demo. Deterministic code does the reliable work; Apertus plans, enriches and answers, and a deterministic validator has the final word on everything it produces.

data.longtext: Swiss parliaments publish a huge amount of open data in different languages, but there is no unified topic assignment across parliaments; it's hugely scattered, and some of them are missing topics entirely. At the same time, labeling those documents is really difficult, as different people have to read and judge the topic on their own, which is slow and error-prone. And because of the lack of topics, finding documents on a specific topic is sometimes impossible. aperTOPic is an open service that finds and tags parliamentary affairs by topic, in any language and for any parliament, using either the standard Année Politique Suisse topics or any new topic you type in. Everything is real and nothing is mocked: Apertus turns your question into search terms in all four languages, OpenParlData returns the live affairs, and the classifier shows a confidence for each topic that a person can correct. With four more weeks, we would tag every affair on OpenParlData, train our own classifier models, check for bias between languages, regions and parties, and test the results with Digital Administration Switzerland against its manual list.

data.name: ParlTopic
data.summary: Every topic. Every parliament. With the evidence.
data.excerpt: # Token Tell -- Making Parliamentary Debates Discoverable ## The Problem OpenParlData provides access to over 300,000 parliamentary affairs across Switzerland and Liechtenstein. However, traditional keyword search misses relevant documents when different terminology or languages are used. The challenge is to enable consistent, multilingual topic classification across parliaments. ## Our Solution Token Tell uses the Swiss open-weight AI model Apertus to classify parliamentary ...
data.longtext:
# Token Tell -- Making Parliamentary Debates Discoverable

## The Problem
OpenParlData provides access to over 300,000 parliamentary affairs across Switzerland and Liechtenstein. However, traditional keyword search misses relevant documents when different terminology or languages are used. The challenge is to enable consistent, multilingual topic classification across parliaments.

## Our Solution
Token Tell uses the Swiss open-weight AI model Apertus to classify parliamentary affairs by meaning rather than keywords. Users can define new topics without retraining, making political information easier to discover across German, French and Italian.

## How It Works
Our prototype processes real OpenParlData records and uses Apertus to determine topic relevance. It provides structured classification results and supports reproducible quality and performance evaluation. The classification pipeline and API benchmarks are real; the storytelling animation is illustrative, not a simulation of actual classification results.

## What's Next -- Four More Weeks
We would expand evaluation using labelled DVS and APS datasets, improve multilingual accuracy and recall, optimise inference costs and processing speed, and integrate topic-based search directly into OpenParlData. Our long-term goal is a scalable, transparent and sovereign AI solution for accessible parliamentary information.

data.longtext:
1. The problem
OpenParlData.ch gives one open API to more than 300,000 affairs from about 90 Swiss parliaments, but they are found mainly by full-text search. Topic labels exist only in pockets: each parliament or project uses its own scheme, often tagged by hand, so a classification made for one purpose cannot be reused for another. In the case partner's words, "its thematic structure is not reusable as a shared resource". Digital Public Services Switzerland (DVS), for example, finds digitalisation affairs through manually assigned tags.

2. Our solution
Parlamentsthemen is an open topic service on Apertus. Every topic is a short topic card: the 22 chapters of the Année Politique Suisse scheme, a parliament's own categories, or ad-hoc topics such as digitalisation, Covid-19 or housing. Our model, Apertus-ParlTopics-8B, is Apertus 1.5 8B fine-tuned as a decision model with Kev (a LoRA adapter and a yes/no head, trained for one epoch on 6,728 labelled federal affairs in 1 h 48 min on one GPU). It reads an affair once and answers every card in one pass with a calibrated probability, so a new topic needs a new card, not retraining, and every decision can be inspected: the probability and threshold, the plain-language card, and the supporting passage with a reason. A search page in German, French, Italian and Romansh finds affairs by meaning, filters them by topic, parliament and year, shows the passage and a short reason behind each suggested topic, and reads results aloud. Topics are suggestions: anyone can report one, and reviewers confirm, remove or add topics on the page, next to the model's original decision.

3. How it works
Everything runs on real data: the trained model runs on our own GPUs and has labelled all 49,978 affairs from 2024 to 2026 with all 29 topics and all 318,801 affairs with digitalisation; the other 28 topics for the older affairs are being added, newest first: 79,978 affairs carry all 29 topics so far, and the remaining 238,823 need about 85 GPU-hours. Results are stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector and served by FastAPI and a Next.js page; everything runs in Docker. Evaluation on labelled samples: APS chapters macro AP 0.74, APS topics F1 0.61 and the seven ad-hoc topics F1 0.74 (against blind frontier-model labels); on the complete St. Gallen, Curia Vista and APS chapter test sets it matches Claude Opus 5.5 (micro F1 0.71, 0.70 and 0.63 against 0.70, 0.69 and 0.62); the quality is equal in German, French and Italian (macro AP 0.71, 0.70 and 0.70); combined with an embedding classifier, it is the best of the compared systems on digitalisation (AP 0.49) and Curia Vista (0.76); a monitoring shortlist finds 29 of the 30 affairs on DVS's published list and 97% of the PolitMonitor-tagged digitalisation affairs from 2024 to 2026, at a precision of about 0.18. Bias was checked across languages and regions, and for federal affairs across parties. Not yet in production: the nightly update and its Apache Hop workflow were run by hand, not scheduled; the review mode uses one shared access code; corrections are stored but do not yet retrain the model; no DVS staff have reviewed the results; affairs before 2024 have no separate quality check. A fresh clone runs on a 5,000-affair demo bundle. The "Warum" explanations come from untrained Apertus through the organisers' endpoint, and read-aloud uses ElevenLabs, an external service that is off without a key.

4. The next four weeks
Week 1: schedule the nightly Hop workflow with the trained model and finish the backfill of older affairs. Week 2: review with DVS staff in the new review mode and agree the topic cards. Week 3: feed corrections into recalibration behind an evaluation gate on a held-out period, and monitor topic shares weekly. Week 4: a DVS pilot with the weekly shortlist, measured in review time, useful discoveries and missed known affairs.

**Hack Apertus Bern/Liebefeld — 3rd place**

**Team:** Prakash Aryan, Kaushik Raghupathruni, Vilas Harapanahalli, Vaibhav Motwani
**Challenge:** Topic classification for Swiss parliaments with Apertus — OpenParlData / Berner Fachhochschule BFH
**The WIN:** CHF 1,000 · ElevenLabs 3 months Pro tier ($297 value/team member, 600k credits/mo) · $50 Hugging Face credits · DINAconCH conference ticket, T-shirt & demo table

**What the team built:**
Every topic of every scheme is written as a short topic card. Apertus 1.5 8B, trained as a decision model (Apertus-ParlTopics-8B), reads an affair once and returns one score per card in a single pass; scores are calibrated where labelled earlier affairs exist. APS chapters, a canton's categories and an ad-hoc topic such as digitalisation are sets of cards that operators add, so a new topic needs no retraining (its threshold still needs validation). Stored results come from Apertus-ParlTopics-8B: all 29 topics for the 49,978 affairs from 2024 to 2026, and digitalisation for all 318,801 affairs; the other 28 topics for the older affairs are being added. Live decisions for affairs without stored results come from Apertus-ParlTopics-8B when its server is configured (PARLTOPICS_DECISION_URL), otherwise from untrained Apertus 1.5 8B; the "Warum" explanations use untrained Apertus 1.5 8B through the LLM_* endpoint.

Source: https://hackapertus.ch/regions/bern-liebefeld

data.summary: Find every Swiss parliamentary affair on your topic — in German, French and Italian — with the sentence that proves it
data.excerpt: THE PROBLEM Switzerland has parliaments at three levels, and OpenParlData collects over 300,000 of their affairs in German, French and Italian --- but there is no shared way to organise them by topic. Monitors such as PolitMonitor, the source of the Digital Public Services Switzerland (DVS) digitalisation list, read and tag affairs by hand. data.longtext:
THE PROBLEM
Switzerland has parliaments at three levels, and OpenParlData collects over 300,000 of their affairs in German, French and Italian --- but there is no shared way to organise them by topic. Monitors such as PolitMonitor, the source of the Digital Public Services Switzerland (DVS) digitalisation list, read and tag affairs by hand. Keyword search misses affairs that never use the word (an e-ID law or a cybersecurity motion may never say "digital"), and the parliaments' own categories don't fit: the closest federal subject area is right only 41% of the time.

OUR SOLUTION
Unisono lets anyone type a topic and a one-line definition --- "digitalisation", "wolf", anything --- or pick a standard scheme (Année Politique Suisse, Curia Vista). Apertus reads every affair in its own language and suggests matches, each with a confidence and one sentence copied from the affair as proof. A human confirms or rejects each suggestion; confirmed lists export to Excel, and "What's new" shows only affairs added since the last visit.

HOW IT WORKS
OpenParlData API → clean text per affair → Apertus v1.5 70B (strict JSON: label, confidence, evidence) → plain Python verifies the evidence sentence really exists in the source (no verified proof, nothing shown) → SQLite → web app with human review. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint; runs on-premise or air-gapped in Docker, no closed model. Everything is real: three whole parliaments since 2018 are indexed (federal 27,465 affairs, Bern 5,249, Thurgau 1,447) and measured against PolitMonitor's manual tags. Bern: 68% precision / 68% recall vs 33% / 47% for keyword search; federal: 63% precision, 22 points above the official subject area. 269 tagged affairs were found that contain no core keyword. Nothing is mocked; without a model endpoint the app shows pre-computed results from these real runs. Limits we state openly: federal recall is 51%, APS accuracy is unmeasured (no answer key), and the blind review was done by one team member.

WHAT'S NEXT (FOUR MORE WEEKS)
Index all 90 parliaments (~19-28 h per topic, measured); a daily "What's new" feed for monitors; an independent second reviewer and an APS answer key to measure what we can't yet; reviewer accounts so every confirmation is attributed; and highlighting the proof sentence in official translations too.

data.name: Thalabus
data.summary: Multi-RAG for parliaments: category, semantic and graph search — every answer cited, no cloud needed
data.excerpt: The problem. Swiss parliamentary data is rich but structurally incomplete: records are published as separate documents even when they concern the same affair. To answer a question, a clerk must find the original question, the committee or council material that followed, and the response --- while ignoring documents that merely share a person, institution or topic. Retrieval is not weak; whole elements are missing. My solution. A browser-based multi-RAG application over a ...
data.longtext:
The problem. Swiss parliamentary data is rich but structurally incomplete: records are published as separate documents even when they concern the same affair. To answer a question, a clerk must find the original question, the committee or council material that followed, and the response --- while ignoring documents that merely share a person, institution or topic. Retrieval is not weak; whole elements are missing.

My solution. A browser-based multi-RAG application over a parliamentary knowledge graph. Three lanes feed one answer --- ontology-constrained categories, semantic chunk search, graph-affinity with shared-entity discovery, and a citation-anchored answer. Proposals and assignments are separate states, so the machine's output never silently becomes the record.

How it works. Real: 39 source PDFs plus a live 40-document dossier ingested into Neo4j; ontology-constrained categorisation (49 definitions --- 27 approved, 22 proposed with zero assignments, so the approval gate holds); simple and advanced chat with citations; case study Kleine Anfrage 2024/26 (9 documents). No screen mockups, no synthetic data.

If I had four more weeks... (1) Extend Dataset: complete the document extraction with a larger sample (e.g. multiple Cantons and some federal-level ones), and capture a live advanced-vs-simple comparison on a small labelled question set (2) Proof of Concept: identify more real cases where knowledge graph links are at advantage over traditional RAG; then compare results with traditional RAG and highlight differences (3) Standardize: check available categorization standards from national and international organizations, if they can be re-used for the Swiss open parlament data (4) Performance: experiment categorization with fast classifier models in a hybrid approach. For example, the recently released Jev has an error rate around 60%-80%. Use it for "simple cases" covering up to 60%-80% of the data sample, and another method for the remaining ones (5) Knowledge Graph Metamodel: improve the graph based on interviews with open parlament data experts (human) (6) Knowledge Graph Algorithm: implement hierarchies as described in my video (7) Knowledge Graph RAG Traversal: on basis of more complete dataset (see 1 above) experiment other graph traversal techniques than the already implemented simplistic approach. (8) Available Categories: analyse already provided categories to merge, extend, re-use when possible

data.longtext:
The problem, in OpenParlData's words. OpenParlData collects 300,000+ affairs from 90 Swiss parliaments, but «today: full-text search only». Users «must anticipate the terminology used in the documents ... and repeat that in every language», so «a simple question like "What did Swiss parliaments decide on digitalisation?" means a lot of manual work». And «the data is available. Its thematic structure is not available as a shared, reusable resource.»

Our solution. Ask once, «digitalisation», and find the affairs on it at every level, federal, cantonal and communal, in German, French and Italian, 88.5% of them with the sentence behind their topic. Querschnitt can tag any affair with any scheme: Année Politique Suisse chapters, a new topic written as one sentence, or a parliament's own scheme as a file. No retraining. On unseen federal affairs, six in ten pass on their own, 82% of them right; the rest go to a person, one keystroke to confirm. Production now runs on Apertus v1.5 70B on CSCS in Switzerland: 3.7 minutes per 1,000 affairs for the topic decisions; the whole archive of 326,123 affairs projected at about 20 hours (USD 893 at Public AI's list price). See it as a static snapshot: https://querschnitt.mi11ion.io

How it works, and what is real. Apertus only ever answers with a listed code, read from its next-token probabilities, so it cannot invent a label. Every quote is checked against the text and stored with its exact position. Measured against human labels, pre-registered:
- APS chapters, 927 federal affairs never used while building: 70.0% right on the first answer; 61.9% decided without a person, 82.4% of those right. Plain list prompting: 65.4%; a TF-IDF classifier trained on the same 1,654 labels: 56.3%; keywords: 18.6%.
- Three languages: the same 400 affairs read in German, French and Italian against the Parliamentary Services' 28 subject areas, the top choice one of the affair's areas: 79.2% / 76.0% / 79.2%, no significant gap (keywords 39.0% / 41.7% / 34.7%).
- A parliament's own scheme, with the five most similar of its own labelled affairs as examples: St. Gallen 77.7%, Stadt Zug 69.7%, Thurgau 59.0% (keywords 32.0% / 53.2% / 26.0%).
- The deck's slide, federal affairs since 2018: Querschnitt is more precise than Curia's hand-made field «Medien und Kommunikation» (55.6% against 40.8%; recall 52.6% against 80.8%), and works where no such field exists: in cantonal and communal parliaments.
- 35 parliaments against PolitMonitor's tag «Digitalisierung»: recall 72.0% (keywords 66.9%), precision at least 34.2%, untagged affairs counting as wrong (keywords 28.9%).

Real: every number above, with its result file in the repo; the scored snapshot with nearly every affair since January 2025, scored via Public AI's Apertus route, which by replay serves the same 70B (the same chapter accuracy as CSCS on the 927 test affairs, the same Digitalisierung decision on 99.9% of 6,425 federal affairs); live classification of any affair from the OpenParlData API (command line and service); a read API, a Postgres migration and an Apache Hop loader, tested in CI; a nightly update from OpenParlData's exports, run daily 14-18 Oct, packaged as one 173 MB image. Not live: the public site is a static snapshot, and its new-topic demo replays a recorded run.

Prepared in the days before the event on public data, building on our online-track work: the engine, the evaluation suite and the app. Built here: production on CSCS and every test on the labelled data handed out at the event.

With four more weeks. A pilot with Digital Public Services Switzerland (DVS) that feeds its manual digitalisation list, with the hours saved measured; the nightly on OpenParlData's server; the whole archive scored; APS's current 22-chapter scheme as the default; and the merge request with OpenParlData.

data.name: Research & Expertise Navigator
data.summary: Connect companies with research expertise at the University of Bern, ARTORG and Diabetes Center Berne
data.excerpt: The Bern Economic Development Agency receives about 300 confidential company leads a year, sometimes several a day. data.longtext:
1. The problem, in the case partner's words
The Bern Economic Development Agency gets about 300 confidential company leads a year, sometimes several a day. Each one needs the right research partner, and in their words, "finding expertise often requires knowing where to search before knowing what to search for." The answer might sit on a faculty site, an institute page, a group profile or a project description. The company's words rarely match the page: someone looking for "glucose sensors" misses pages that say "continuous glucose monitoring", "biosensing" or "CGM".

Three things from the workshop shaped the build. The company document is confidential: "we cannot put it onto any model." The pitch has to be honest: "we cannot oversell, we must sell what we have." And every statement needs a reference: "where can I check that?" Other cantons pitch the same company, so speed and credibility decide whether Bern gets the visit.

2. Our solution
Mutz turns a company's one-pager into the right experts in Bern, and every claim links to its source page. The officer pastes the brief, uploads a PDF, gives a website or types keywords. Mutz pulls out the company's needs, finds ranked expertise for each one, and gives a plain reason and the quote behind it. When Bern has nothing strong, it says "no match" and lists what it searched. The officer accepts the suggestions, and the accepted ones become an A4 pitch in EN, DE or FR. Every card has to be ticked before the PDF leaves. Our rule: Apertus reads and writes, code checks every quote.

How it works, and what is real vs mocked:
- Crawl: a polite crawl of 3,026 pages from 16 sites (ARTORG, Diabetes Center Berne and 14 UniBE institutes).
- Extraction: Apertus 8B pulls out people, units, projects and infrastructure. A fact enters the knowledge graph only if its quote is real: 19,631 facts have a source.
- Search: BM25 plus BGE-M3 in DE, EN and FR, with lay-term expansion from Apertus 70B, a local cross-encoder and an Apertus 70B judge per unit, so small groups still show up.
- Swiss hosting: Apertus runs on CSCS. Embeddings and reranking run inside our container, and confidential parts of the brief (revenue, salaries, contacts) are removed locally before anything is sent.
- More data: SNSF grants come from the open data. Mutz the bear is a chat assistant that uses the same functions as the UI.
- Evaluation: on 23 held-out questions we never tuned on, 91% have a right expert in the top 10. Recall@10 is 89% against an 80% target.

Running it: there is a live demo and a one-command Docker image.

Mocked or simplified:
- Demo leads: the demo company and the other demo leads are invented. The gap report and capability map run on seeded test data, labelled as demo on screen.
- Sending: "Send" exports the PDFs, and outreach and the visit day are drafts plus an .ics file.
- New sources: "Add a source" writes to the config, but someone still runs the crawl by hand.
- Data freshness: the crawl is a one-off; talent needs are answered from a hand-checked list of Bern programmes, and supplier needs are marked "not covered yet".
- Logins: officers pick their name with no password, and the demo sits behind basic auth.
- Air-gapped setup: it's prepared but not tested. Cost per case (about 35k tokens) is an estimate.
- What the score means: Recall@10 is evaluated on cases we picked ourselves, so it doesn't show whether a company would find them useful.

4. What's next with four more weeks
- Week 1: a pilot with the agency's officers on real, anonymised leads, using their accept/reject clicks as labels for evaluation.
- Week 2: cover the rest of the UniBE inventory (we crawl 14 of 42 sites), plus Insel and sitem-insel. Add a scheduled re-crawl, checked automatically, with alerts when new matching research appears.
- Week 3: fill the supplier gap with suppliers and manufacturers. Add a way for researchers to correct or remove what we show about them.
- Week 4: run Apertus 70B on our own air-gapped setup, and add real logins. Hand the agency a gap report built from real lead data instead of test rows.

data.longtext:
Description:
1. The Problem
"Today, finding expertise often requires knowing where to search before knowing what to search for. Information is distributed across a large and heterogeneous landscape of institutional websites (UniBE, ARTORG, Diabetes Center Berne). On top of that, the terminology used by the person searching may differ significantly from the terminology used on the source website (e.g., 'glucose sensors' vs. 'continuous glucose monitoring'). The challenge is to transform this fragmented web landscape into a unified, semantically searchable knowledge resource."

2. Our Solution
We built the Research & Expertise Navigator, an end-to-end AI-powered search engine that unifies distributed web sources across the University of Bern, ARTORG Center, and Diabetes Center Berne into a single natural-language search interface. It bridges vocabulary gaps between laypersons and academics, delivering structured, 100% traceable result cards with direct back-links to verifiable source pages.

3. How It Works
Data Ingestion (scraper.py): Crawls seed URLs across UniBE subdomains, ARTORG, and DCB, stripping boilerplate HTML to preserve core content.
LLM Structured Extraction & Enrichment (database.py): Apertus 70B (apertus-v1-5-70b) parses web pages to extract researchers, roles, units, expertise, projects, and infrastructure, while generating 5-10 layperson synonyms per profile.
Semantic Retrieval & Dynamic Query Expansion (main.py): User queries are expanded in real time via Apertus 70B to include academic synonyms, then matched using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 dense vectors stored in a local persistent ChromaDB collection.
LLM Verification Bouncer (main.py): Every candidate result passes through an Apertus verification prompt to generate a 1-sentence match justification and eliminate hallucinations before reaching the user.
Real vs. Mocked: Everything in this prototype is 100% real and functional end-to-end. The crawler, vector indexer, query expander, LLM verification bouncer, and FastAPI backend are live. A pre-indexed vector database snapshot is included solely to ensure instantaneous search responses during live evaluations.

4. What Is Next (With 4 More Weeks)
Automated Continuous Ingestion: Scheduled background webhooks to detect institutional updates and incrementally update vector records without re-crawling.
Multilingual Processing: Native cross-lingual alignment (German, French, and English) to handle search queries in any official Swiss language seamlessly.
Air-Gapped Apertus 8B On-Premise Engine: Fine-tune and quantize the local Apertus 8B model to run embedding generation and verification completely offline without external gateway dependencies.
Interactive Collaboration Visualizer: A visual graph interface mapping cross-departmental research networks, shared infrastructure, and active interdisciplinary projects.

data.longtext:
The problem, in the case partner's words: "Today, finding expertise often requires knowing where to search before knowing what to search for." Expertise is scattered across faculty sites, institute pages, group profiles and project pages. And the words don't match: someone searching "glucose sensors" misses pages that say CGM, biosensing or continuous glucose monitoring. The Agency asked for one searchable view of UniBE, ARTORG and Diabetes Center Berne, with every answer traceable to its source.

Our solution
Bern Expertise Navigator (bern-expertise.ch). An officer writes down what a company needs. The platform searches the three institutions and comes back with people, labs, projects and facilities, each one linked to the page and the sentence it came from. An officer checks every suggestion before anything leaves the system. From there it helps draft a short pitch and an invitation to Bern. When the evidence is thin, it says so instead of guessing.

What's real, what isn't
Working: the crawler for all three sites (2,386 entities indexed, plus OpenAlex), hybrid search with keywords and local multilingual embeddings, a checker that deletes any field it can't find in the source text, abstention on weak matches, and the staff workspace with leads, review and pitch drafting. It all runs in Docker on local models, no external AI API. Apertus handles messy pages, extraction, term expansion and the match explanations; when it falls back to rules, the UI shows it. On our own test set: recall@10 90%, traceability 100%, abstention 100%. Those numbers are rules-only, no Apertus yet, and we wrote the test queries from the pages we indexed, so read them as optimistic. Lay-term matching is weak at 5 of 10 pairs. Auth and deployment are hackathon-grade. No Agency officer has used it on a real request.

Four more weeks
Week 1 we'd rerun everything on fresh queries, benchmark Apertus 8B and 70B against the rules baseline, and measure what it costs to run. Week 2, two or three officers try it on real requests. Week 3 we fix whatever broke. Week 4 is auth, hosting and a runbook, then a go/no-go on a pilot together.

data.longtext:
1. The problem
The Bern Economic Development Agency describes the challenge as "knowing where to search before knowing what to search for." Research expertise is scattered across websites, and companies often use different words from researchers. Someone looking for "glucose sensors" may miss relevant work described as "continuous glucose monitoring."

2. Our solution
Our Research & Expertise Navigator helps advisors find relevant research in Bern using everyday language. It brings together public information from the University of Bern, ARTORG and Diabetes Center Berne, explains potential matches and links each claim to its source. Advisors review the results before exporting a company-facing brief.

3. How it works
The system collects public research pages and organizes their content. Apertus interprets the company's needs, helps find relevant evidence and drafts an explanation. The backend checks supporting passages and keeps missing information visible. The search, database, AI processing and reviewed PDF export are implemented and have run with real sources and connected services. The repeatable HelioSense demo uses a fictional company and scripted results to demonstrate the interface. Search quality at broader scale and fully offline deployment still need validation.

4. With four more weeks
We would work closely with agency advisors, gather feedback on real cases and improve the tool around their daily needs. We would add automatic source updates, support more research fields and introduce shared team workflows for reviewing and handing over cases. User testing would guide which features we build first.

**Hack Apertus Bern/Liebefeld — 2nd place**

**Team:** Renato Mignone, Elia Innocenti, Mohamed Kechiche, Eric Ruiz Giménez
**Challenge:** Research & Expertise Navigator — Bern Economic Development Agency
**The WIN:** CHF 2,500 · ElevenLabs 3 months Pro tier ($297 value/team member, 600k credits/mo) · $100 Hugging Face credits · DINAconCH conference ticket, T-shirt & demo table

**What the team built:**
- Understands intent: Apertus v1.5 maps everyday wording to a reviewed domain vocabulary while preserving the company's full needs and constraints.
- Searches one ecosystem: independent PostgreSQL full-text and pgvector retrieval, RRF fusion, optional reranking and connected public web research.
- Makes findings inspectable: exact passages, original URLs, source status, direct/adjacent fit and explicit missing information.
- Keeps the operator in control: durable chat/revisions, keep/reject review and exact-hash approval before deterministic PDF or enabled PowerPoint export.

Source: https://hackapertus.ch/regions/bern-liebefeld

The problem. In the case partner's words, "finding expertise often requires knowing where to search before knowing what to search for", and "the searcher's words often differ from the source's". A search for "glucose sensors" misses pages that say CGM or biosensing.

Our solution. Bern Life is a Research & Expertise Navigator inside a small life-sim of Bern. Ask in English, German or French, on the phone, at the office computer or through Lumi, your bear agent. You get people, units, projects and facilities from UniBE, ARTORG and DCB. Every fact is a sentence quoted from the institution's page, with its link. With no source, it says so.

How it works. Real: 3,351 public pages crawled. Apertus v1.5 70B proposes values, and code keeps only those whose sentence is verbatim on the page (3,484 profiles). Search is hybrid, in Postgres/pgvector. Model calls are cached, so make run replays with no GPU and make live-run calls Apertus live. Accounts, messages, map walking and the Exoscale hosting all work. Mocked: demo data only with DEMO_FIXTURES=1, labelled. Unrecorded questions run as plain search, also labelled. The city is drawn.

Results. recall@10 0.39 [0.24, 0.56] against 0.80. 100% of claims traceable, 0 invented. 9 of 10 invented questions refused, with no false refusals.

Next four weeks. Group pages as units and topic claims for name-only people, the two stages where most recall is lost. Then better German and French matching, a correction workflow, and more institutions at one JSON file each.
